concept.name: Normal yield curve
concept.definition: A yield curve configuration in which longer-maturity yields are higher than shorter-maturity yields, giving the curve an upward slope. It is the historically most common configuration, reflecting term premia and typical expectations that rates will not fall sharply.
concept.intuition: Lenders usually demand more compensation for tying up money longer, so longer loans carry higher rates — that is the 'normal' state of the curve.
concept.mechanics: The slope is measured as a spread between constant-maturity yields, e.g. the 10-year minus the 2-year Treasury yield; a positive value corresponds to a normal (upward-sloping) curve.
concept.formula: Slope ≈ y(long maturity) − y(short maturity) > 0, e.g. 10-year CMT minus 2-year CMT.
concept.failure_modes: An upward slope does not prove rates will rise; the slope conflates term premium, rate expectations, and issuance/demand effects, so reading it as a pure forecast is unreliable.
concept.misconceptions: It is wrong to assume 'normal' means guaranteed or stable; curves can steepen or flatten quickly, and a normal curve is simply the modal historical shape, not a law.
concept.example: If 3-month bills yield 3.5%, the 2-year note yields 4.0%, and the 10-year yields 4.5%, the curve is normal (upward sloping).
